sections.title: Growth & Margin Expansion
sections.subtitle: Revenue has been flat-to-declining for three years; the entire recent profit story is gross-margin expansion from 'Back to Basics' cost discipline and pricing

charts.title: Gross Margin
charts.annotation: Both FY and half-year points are shown on the FY/interim toggle. FY: 15.8% (FY2013) to 26.5% (FY2025). H1 FY2026: 33.7%, up from 28.2% in H1 FY2025 -- three consecutive halves of expansion.

sections.title: Cash Flow & Earnings Quality
sections.subtitle: The DCF's central argument: FY2025's record cash flow does not repeat at the same rate as it converts into working capital

charts.title: Operating Cash Flow vs Net Income
charts.annotation: FY2025 OCF was $135.3m against NPAT of $63.7m (strong conversion, partly a $22m cash-tax underpayment now unwinding). H1 FY2026 OCF collapsed to $13.7m against NPAT of $42.4m as earnings were absorbed into frozen mussel inventory -- the single most important risk signal in this dashboard. Toggle to H1/H2 view to see the H1 FY2026 print directly.

charts.title: Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF (Base Case)
charts.annotation: Reported FCF (from the CSV) goes negative in several early years, so this chart cannot use a log scale. It swings from near-zero or negative through most of FY2013-FY2024 to a peak of $112.9m in FY2025. The DCF strips out SBC and lease payments to get owner FCF of $96.2m for FY2025 -- 6.4x the FY2016-FY2025 median (~$15m) -- and treats it as a peak: the model's year-1 (FY2026E) owner FCF is $74.2m, fading to a $41-50m mid-cycle by the outer projection years as margins, capex and working capital normalise (see the DCF Valuation section below for the full path).

charts.title: CapEx
charts.annotation: FY2025 capex of $22.5m (3.9% of revenue) and H1 FY2026's $6.7m are deferral-level lows against a 10-year average near 8% -- the DCF normalizes capex up to 6% of revenue by year 5 given the aging fleet's five-year dry-dock cycle.

sections.title: Balance Sheet & Capital
sections.subtitle: Quota (carried at historic cost, not fair value) is the durable underlying asset; net debt has been cut sharply since FY2024

charts.title: Total Debt vs Shareholders' Equity
charts.annotation: Shareholders' equity (~$740m at FY2025, ~$780m at H1 FY2026) includes roughly $486m of fishing-quota intangibles carried at HISTORIC COST under NZ IFRS, not fair or replacement value -- book equity, and any P/B-style comparison drawn from it, understates the true asset backing. Net debt fell from $185.5m (FY2024-end) to $93.4m (FY2025-end) before rising to $102.1m at H1 FY2026 on the mussel inventory build.

charts.title: EPS (cents)
charts.annotation: EPS is reported in the CSV in CENTS (FY2025 = 68.1, meaning NZ$0.681), not dollars -- do not read the raw number as a dollar figure. EPS more than tripled from 21.1c (FY2024) to 68.1c (FY2025) on the same profit surge described in the Net Income and Gross Margin charts. The dividend (DividendPerShare column, in whole NZ dollars, e.g. 0.05 = 5.0 cents) has been held flat at 5.0 cents per half through FY2025 and the HY26 interim as the Board prioritises debt paydown over payout growth -- roughly 7% of EPS at the FY2025 run rate.

charts.title: EBITDA
charts.annotation: FY2025 EBITDA of $141.0m is a record, but includes non-cash biological fair-value gains on the salmon book; the DCF strips these out for its projected margins (see Cash Flow section).

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Total sales revenue across Sanford's three pillars: Wildcatch (deepwater and inshore quota fishing -- hoki, scampi, orange roughy, squid, toothfish, plus inshore ACE leasing to Moana New Zealand), Aquaculture Salmon (King Salmon farmed at Big Glory Bay, Stewart Island) and Greenshell Mussels (Marlborough and Coromandel). Volume is largely fixed by the Quota Management System and consented farm space, so revenue moves mainly with realised commodity prices and mix.

For Sanford: revenue has been essentially flat for three years ($582.9m FY2024, $584.1m FY2025, and H1 FY2026 down 5.5% year-on-year to $270.2m). The 10-year CAGR is only 2.8%. Both wildcatch (QMS-capped, with the ORH 3B orange roughy TACC just cut 51%) and salmon (Big Glory Bay's nitrogen-discharge ceiling) have explicit no-growth outlooks from management for FY2026; mussels (Western Firth of Thames consent, new vessel, SPATnz hatchery) is the only near-term volume-growth lever.

What to watch:

  • Whether mussel volume growth (first Western Firth harvest ~March 2027) offsets flat wildcatch and salmon
  • Realised price moves in scampi (China demand), hoki (Northern Hemisphere pollock pricing) and orange roughy (TACC-scarcity pricing)

grossMargin.title: Gross Margin
grossMargin.content:
Gross profit (revenue less cost of revenue) as a percentage of revenue -- the cleanest read on pricing, cost discipline and processing yield before overheads.

For Sanford: this is the single most important chart on this dashboard. Gross margin has expanded from 15.8% (FY2013) through 21.6% (FY2024) to 26.5% (FY2025) and 33.7% (H1 FY2026) -- three consecutive halves of improvement, credited by management to SKU rationalisation, a 'push to pull' supply-chain model and Havelock mussel-factory yield gains. The DCF treats roughly half of this gain as structural (fading the EBITDA margin to a 20% mid-cycle versus the 15.7% decade average and FY2025's 24.1% ex-gain), because FY2025/H1 FY2026 were also flattered by an unusually favourable mussel harvest yield that management itself says will not repeat at the same level.

What to watch:

  • Whether margin holds above 25% through FY2026 as mussel yields normalise from FY2025's exceptional level (management guides 'above average but not repeating FY25')
  • The wildcatch strategic review outcome, which could reshape the cost base further

operatingMargin.title: Operating & Net Margin
operatingMargin.content:
Operating income and net income as percentages of revenue, tracking how much of the gross-margin gain survives overheads, interest and tax.

For Sanford: operating margin reached 17.5% in FY2025 and 23.7% in H1 FY2026, both records, moving in lockstep with the gross-margin expansion. Net margin lags operating margin by the interest and tax lines; falling net debt (interest cost down from $16.9m to $12.1m) is now adding a second tailwind on top of the gross-margin story.

What to watch:

  • The gap between operating and net margin narrowing further as debt paydown continues
  • Whether H1 FY2026's non-cash $17.5m salmon biological fair-value gain (versus $3.3m a year earlier) is inflating the operating margin print for that half

cashConversion.title: Operating Cash Flow vs Net Income
cashConversion.content:
Operating cash flow (cash actually generated by the business) compared against net income (the accounting profit) for the same period. A business converting profit into cash should show these two lines moving together; a persistent gap is a working-capital or earnings-quality flag.

For Sanford: this is the DCF's central risk argument made visible. FY2025 looked like excellent conversion -- OCF $135.3m against NPAT $63.7m -- but part of that was a $22m cash-tax underpayment (cash tax paid just $3.3m against ~$25m accrued) that had to catch up eventually. It did: H1 FY2026 OCF collapsed to just $13.7m against NPAT of $42.4m, as growing profit was absorbed into a build-up of frozen half-shell mussel inventory (weak US/China demand meant product could not be sold through as fast as it was produced) and the deferred tax bill was paid ($17.5m in the half).

What to watch:

  • Whether H2 FY2026 sees the frozen mussel inventory clear and OCF recover toward NPAT
  • This gap is exactly why the DCF does not simply capitalise FY2025's reported free cash flow -- it treats FY2025 as a peak and fades to a lower mid-cycle owner FCF

fcf.title: Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF (Base Case)
fcf.content:
Reported Free Cash Flow (operating cash flow less capital expenditure, as filed) compared against the DCF's projected owner free cash flow -- reported FCF further adjusted for stock-based compensation and lease principal/interest payments.

For Sanford: reported FCF swings from negative in several years (FY2013-FY2023 averaged close to zero, with multiple negative years during capex-heavy periods) to a peak of $112.9m in FY2025. The DCF's owner FCF (after stripping SBC of $0.2m and lease payments of ~$16.4m) was $96.2m for FY2025 -- 6.4x the FY2016-FY2025 median of roughly $15m. Because this is clearly a peak (working-capital release plus the cash-tax underpayment described above), the model does not capitalise it: year-1 (FY2026E) owner FCF is projected at $74.2m, fading to a $41-50m mid-cycle by the outer years as margins, capex and working capital normalise.

What to watch:

  • Reported FCF cannot use a log scale (it goes negative in several years) -- read the absolute levels, not ratios
  • The DCF line only starts at FY2026E; it is a forecast, not a historical actual

capex.title: CapEx
capex.content:
Cash capital expenditure on vessels, processing plant and farm infrastructure.

For Sanford: capex has been unusually low recently -- $22.5m in FY2025 (3.9% of revenue) and just $6.7m in H1 FY2026 -- as management deliberately prioritised debt paydown over investment while the wildcatch/aquaculture strategic review was underway. This is well below the roughly 8% of revenue the fleet has averaged over ten years, and below total depreciation and amortisation (6.1% of revenue), meaning the asset base is arguably being run down. The aging fleet (some vessels 30+ years old) faces five-year dry-dock recertification cycles that will eventually force capex back up.

What to watch:

  • Whether capex re-accelerates once the strategic review concludes and the mussel growth pipeline (Western Firth of Thames, new vessel) moves into construction
  • The DCF ramps base-case capex from 3.5% to 6.0% of revenue by year 5 to reflect this normalisation

debtEquity.title: Total Debt vs Shareholders' Equity
debtEquity.content:
Total interest-bearing debt against total shareholders' equity at each period end.

For Sanford: net debt was cut aggressively from $185.5m (FY2024-end) to $93.4m (FY2025-end) as the Back to Basics program prioritised balance-sheet repair, before rising modestly to $102.1m at H1 FY2026 on the mussel inventory build. Shareholders' equity of roughly $740-780m includes about $486m of fishing-quota intangibles carried at HISTORIC COST under NZ IFRS -- not fair or replacement value. This means book equity, and any price-to-book comparison built from it, understates Sanford's true asset backing; the stock has closed above 1.0x book in only four of the last ten fiscal years (FY2016-FY2019), which the DCF's own valuation philosophy treats as evidence the market prices earnings power rather than the quota's replacement value, not as a mispricing to be arbitraged.

What to watch:

  • Continued debt reduction from the $102.1m H1 FY2026 level as management has explicitly guided
  • The refinanced $140m bank facility (reduced from $160m, completed 31 March 2026) reflecting the lower ongoing debt requirement

epsDividend.title: EPS vs Dividend per Share
epsDividend.content:
Earnings per share against dividend declared per share, both shown in NZ cents.

For Sanford: EPS is reported in the CSV in CENTS (FY2025 = 68.1, meaning NZ$0.681), not dollars -- do not read the raw number as a dollar figure. EPS more than tripled from 21.1c (FY2024) to 68.1c (FY2025) on the same profit surge described in the Net Income and Gross Margin charts. The dividend, by contrast, has been held flat at 5.0 cents per half (interim and final) through FY2025 and into the HY26 interim, as the Board explicitly prioritises 'a conservative dividend profile ... strengthening the company's balance sheet' over faster payout growth.

What to watch:

  • Whether dividend growth resumes once net debt reduction and the wildcatch strategic review are further advanced
  • The widening gap between EPS and DPS as a sign of increasing retained-earnings reinvestment, not a warning sign on its own

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, as reported.

For Sanford: FY2025 EBITDA of $141.0m is a record (up from $108.7m in FY2024), tracking the same gross-margin expansion driving every other profitability line. It includes non-cash biological fair-value gains on the salmon book (H1 FY2026 alone carried a $17.5m gain versus $3.3m in H1 FY2025) that the DCF strips out when building its own projected margins, since these are mark-to-market movements on livestock, not cash operating profit.

What to watch:

  • The ex-biological-gain EBITDA margin (roughly 23.8% in H1 FY2026 versus a 30.3% reported figure) is the more reliable read on operating performance
  • The DCF's mid-cycle EBITDA margin assumption of 20% versus the FY2025 reported 24.1%, reflecting an expectation that some of the recent gain proves cyclical
